newsitem.title: BRAZIL: U.S. plays hardball at Americas trade talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plays hardball at Americas trade talks.

text.p: The United States took a tough stance on Friday at a key ministerial free-trade meeting, warning its partners in the Americas it might "pack its bags" unless a deal were struck, Brazilian government sources said.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said she could not sign the draft declaration that had been prepared for her and ministers from Canada to Argentina meeting to discuss setting up the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
"If we remain in this half-way zone, it would be better to pack our bags and go home," Barshefsky said, according to a Brazilian government source with access to the meeting.
The top U.S. trade official was addressing trade and foreign ministers from 33 other countries in the region meeting in Belo Horizonte to decide when to start formal negotiations for the FTAA.
Launched at a Miami summit in 1994, the FTAA envisioned a free trade zone of nearly one billion consumers and combined gross domestic product of over $9.0 trillion.
"This declaration (in Belo Horizonte) is inconsistent with what happened in Miami. We are trying to rewrite Miami and this cannot be agreed to by the United States," Barshefsky said.
Despite Barshefsky's hardball approach, other officials were still optimistic about reaching a deal on Friday.
Argentine Foreign Minister Guido di Tella told Argentine journalists later that a deal had been struck on the most controversial of the sticking points.
"By this evening we will have got rid of all the brackets (in the declaration)," di Tella said, referring to the parenthesis placed around words and phrases subject to disagreement.
Sebastiao do Rego Barros, executive secretary of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry, said he was "almost sure" the declaration would be signed on Friday, despite continuing discord.

The Belo Horizonte talks have floundered on a north-south divide, with the United States pushing for speed in negotiating regional free trade and South America's Mercosur trade bloc of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay urging caution.
All would like to start formal talks after a presidential FTAA summit in Chile next March.
But, while Mercosur wants to negotiate in stages, with tariff cuts left until last, the United States wants to discuss everything from tariffs to subsidies at the same time.
"What is going on is a war of equilibrium (between the United States and Mercosur)," said Stefan Bogdan Salej, president of local state industry federation FIEMG.

Argentina's di Tella said the ministers had decided to declare they would be "in a condition" to launch formal talks in March 1998 but would have to reach consensus on key issues of their objectives, stages and structure before then.

Diplomats note the United States' bargaining power in Belo Horizonte has been hamstrung by the Clinton administration's admission that it faced daunting odds in getting so-called "fast track" negotiating authority from Congress this year.
"The irony of this meeting is that the United States has been pressing us to hurry up but they themselves do not have the legislation to advance," di Tella said.
The ministers will also have to decide whether to allow the labour movement a greater role in the process. Business leaders already hold official parallel forums to FTAA meetings.
